- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 247): **Encoding and use are separate quantities and neither alone is evidence of anything, and this paper is the folder's cleanest demonstration because both sides are measured with an oracle: 172 deterministically-labelled concepts are equally decodable at every skill condition (96.0%/95.9% mean probe accuracy, per-concept SD across eleven levels of 0.57 points, cross-skill transfer gap 0.40/0.43 points) while best-move accuracy in the lowest band is 0.144, and freezing the backbone while retraining an 8.2%-parameter head lifts that to 0.828.** The logic that makes it a dissociation rather than two unrelated facts is the direction of the intervention: a linear head can only reweight what the frozen state already contains, so recovery from unchanged representations rules out "the weaker condition lost the knowledge" while the flat probe rules out "the head simply learned a new capability from scratch" — the two controls have to be run together or each explains away the other. Three habits follow. Any claim of the form "feature X is not represented under condition C" needs a probe that transfers across C and an intervention that fails to recover from C's states, because a probe with a separately fitted readout per condition cannot distinguish a shifted representation from an absent one. Any claim that an intervention improved behaviour needs the pre-intervention readout re-measured on the intervened states, since otherwise a representational change and a change in use are indistinguishable. And the specificity control is the one that carries the most weight here: other-concept heads scored *below* the frozen baseline, which is stronger than the usual "no significant gain" and rules out a uniformly better policy in one line. (arxiv-2611.03439, arxiv-2611.11035, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 247): **The control that kills the strongest objection to a retrained-readout experiment is cheap and asymmetric: train the new map only on the *other* condition's states and test it on the target condition, and here that costs almost nothing — a head trained and early-stopped on highest-skill states alone reaches 0.800 in the lowest band against 0.828 for the all-skill head and stays within 2.9 points in every band.** This is the folder's transfer-instead-of-fit discipline (run 239's "train a predictor on one group and score it on the other") arriving with the confound named explicitly: an intervention head fit on the same states it is evaluated on could be memorising those states' idiosyncrasies, and the high-skill-only arm removes that without an ablation or a second model. Two generalisations carry into our own battery. Every recovery claim should print the opposing-condition-only variant beside the pooled one, because the gap between them is the size of the fit, and its smallness is the argument. And the corollary is a reminder about what "the same representation" means: two conditions can differ by a smooth, distance-graded shift (the transfer gap here grows with skill distance, and the extreme corner still reads at 93%) while remaining one linearly readable object — so a small but nonzero representational difference is compatible with full functional availability, and the right question is whether a *fixed* readout survives, not whether the states are identical. (arxiv-2611.03439, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.13548)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 247): **"The representation did not change" is a positive claim and needs an equivalence test with a declared margin, not a failed null — here feature steering still moved probe accuracy by +0.86 points, the paper reports the number, and the equivalence verdict comes from a paired two-one-sided test against a ±1-point margin that was chosen before the comparison.** The distinction is not pedantry: the reader has to know whether the observed shift is small *relative to a stated tolerance* or merely not significant in a sample, and only the first licenses the sentence "the gain in behaviour did not come with a loss of encoding". The same discipline explains why the steering arm is weaker evidence than the head arm even though its effect sizes look comparable — steering edits activations, so preservation of encoding is an empirical result, whereas freezing the trunk makes it true by construction, and the paper says exactly that. Two things to import. State the margin and the test when claiming stability, and prefer constructions where stability is guaranteed when the claim is central. And report the mechanism-versus-site caveat in the same breath: success at the policy head tells you the information was available, not where the model implements the conditioning, since the Elo embeddings enter every block's queries and the head receives none — a recovery site is a probe of availability, never a localisation of the original computation. (arxiv-2611.03439, arxiv-2611.08551, arxiv-2611.04349)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 246): **Offline transfer and closed-loop effect are separate quantities, and this paper's numbers make the gap explicit: a prefill patch of the decision token at layer 16 transfers 0.95 of the first action dimension and at most 0.04 of the other five, yet redirects 0 of 18 rollouts, and every fixed vector or prefill patch at layers 12–20 redirects none of 158, while patching every decoded action token redirects 7 of 18 at layer 16 and 15 of 18 at layer 24.** The mechanism is stated plainly and is the transferable part: the later action tokens still attend to the unedited instruction, so a single-site patch certifies only the *first* downstream step, and the read sites that matter are downstream of the site patched. Three habits follow. Any location claim of the form "position P carries X from layer L" should name the read sites the claim covers, because an autoregressive model re-reads its prompt at every generated token — the folder's previous patching entries all patch a single decision position and inherit this hole. Any edit we publish should be scored in the loop that the behaviour lives in, since the offline normalised logit difference is not a proxy with a stable relationship to it. And the depth boundary has a direction: edits must act *before* the handover (layers 12–16 in OpenVLA) or reach every generated token, which is the same shape as the folder's "word-level edits peak in the first tenth of the network" finding, with a hard operational rule attached. (arxiv-2611.08895, arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.12538)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 246): **A readout can be faithful and useless at once, and the cleanest demonstration is a monitor with perfect recall and a degenerate claim: the goal probe flags all 95 forbidden executions and also all 25 stalls (false-alarm rate 1.00), because it reports the goal *named in the instruction* rather than the goal executed under negation, and accordingly it flags predicted success of the forbidden task — the same behaviour as a keyword rule for "not".** The decomposition is worth importing: a monitor's score has to be computed *against the specification* (largest disallowed log-probability minus largest allowed) for it to mean anything, and even then its usefulness is bounded by whether the model's internal goal says something the instruction does not. Where it does — mid-episode redirects, where the instruction is stale — the same probe reaches within-pair AUROC 0.88, beats a success probe by 0.13 and entropy by 0.29, and the in-sample pair+time prior that looks better pooled (0.96) is constant within a pair and therefore empty by construction. This is the folder's "denominator/conditioning" lesson arriving on the monitoring side, and the cheap tell is the same: a monitor whose score is identical across the conditions you care about is reporting the input, not the model. (arxiv-2611.08895, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.18089)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 246): **An interpretability instrument must beat a cheap external baseline at matched information before it has earned its complexity, and here the external comparator is not close to failing: a DINOv2 image+instruction probe matches the layer-32 internal readout within 0.02 AUROC (interval −0.02 to +0.06) on redirect non-compliance, and a linear probe on privileged object and end-effector poses reaches 0.90 pooled and 0.79 within pair.** Two things generalise. The privileged baseline is the right ceiling to print beside any internal instrument — it bounds what *any* representation of the situation can buy on this task, and here it is beaten within pair by the internal probe (0.88 vs 0.79), which is the only reason the internal access has a story. And the negative half is a result, not a null to be buried: under negation every goal-based monitor is at keyword level, so the paper's recommendation is to enforce prohibitions outside the instruction — an option that exists only because the instrument was honest about where it stops working. For our battery this is the third instance in three runs of the same discipline (a survival count needs a seed floor, a coherence score needs a thresholded null, a monitor needs an external baseline), and it argues for one standing column in every table we publish: the best cheap baseline at matched inputs. (arxiv-2611.08895, arxiv-2611.08551, arxiv-2611.11035)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 245): **A mechanistic claim can be true, complete and not minimal at once, and this paper is the folder's first account that states the reason instead of hedging: no single head moves the answer by more than 0.14 nats against a 1.3-nat margin, twenty heads knocked out on a fresh draw cost −0.74 nats where twenty random heads cost +0.02, and the bound that predicts this is arithmetic — no head writes more than 0.2 nats directly, so a 1.3-nat answer is a sum over at least seven.** The decomposition is the transferable part: where a step needs little output gain the model *concentrates* (two heads compute the query's class, sixteen detect repeats, three key–value groups carry half the label's identity), and where the demand exceeds one head's output-value gain the model *sums*, so the right object is a direction plus a size-matched random-subspace comparison rather than a head list. Llama makes the case sharper by hiding it: a census of 288 heads finds no single head above 0.12 nats and 271 within 0.03, yet the census-ranked twenty-four raise the margin by +1.90 as a set against +0.12 for random. For our own writing this prescribes a sentence we currently cannot write — per step, say whether the model concentrated or summed and give the gain bound — and it retires the two bad options of claiming a responsible head or declaring the phenomenon distributed and closing the question. (arxiv-2611.05344, arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.16315)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 245): **An ablation reference is not a nuisance parameter but the thing that decides whether a completeness test can rank at all, and the demonstration is unusually blunt: replacing every unnamed head with a mean taken over natural text made the named circuit lose everything (−0.79 / −0.88 nats from intact +1.13 / +0.55) and a same-size random set lose exactly as much (−0.83 / −0.79), and keeping *no* heads score the same (−0.82 / −0.81), so the test had no resolution left.** With a mean over distribution-matched prompts the same test ranks the sets, and with the matched set of 189 heads the circuit alone matches or beats the intact model. Two refinements are the ones to carry into our battery: the reference must be matched on *every* factor the claim says is irrelevant — here the label pair as well as the prompts, since a reference mixing label pairs moves results by up to a nat, and the authors' own first version made that mistake and report it — and the position scope of the substitution is part of the claim, because replacing at the query only certifies the readout given intact slots and says nothing about how the slots were built. This is the folder's matched-control rule at its most operational: a control that is unmatched does not produce a weak effect, it produces no effect for the true set and a false null for everything else. (arxiv-2611.05344, arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.25038)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 245): **An algorithm that is conserved across models can be absent from a model trained on the same task, and the variable that decides is whether the *default* behaviour is penalised — the scratch-trained transformer grows the writers, the readers and the slot structure, but the gate appears in four of five seeds only under the distribution where a unique-label prompt carries a fresh unpredictable query, and in the two control distributions the gate direction is at chance (held-out sign accuracy 0.45–0.62) and steering along it does nothing while both prompt kinds are answered with the same margin.** The reading is that the gate is not implied by the task but by the *trade-off* the task sits inside, which reframes every gating, abstention and context-trust mechanism this folder has met: it should be sought where a cheap default would otherwise be right, and its absence from a small model is evidence about that model's fallback, not about its capacity. Two consequences for us. The same test transfers to probes — a direction that separates two conditions is not a mechanism until steering along it changes behaviour, and the natural control is the distribution where the separation exists but does not pay. And the developmental order they observe (copying, then the null action, then class-keyed retrieval; the 1B model never developing the last) is the checkpoint-level version of asking whether a component is present or merely dormant, which is the question our own readouts keep raising about small versus large models. (arxiv-2611.05344, arxiv-2611.03518, arxiv-2611.11035)

Full text, 123,630 clean chars incl. two query heads carry 40% of the query flip with 64% of their write in the readers' match-functional span; twenty readers −0.74 vs random +0.02, twenty-four brakes +1.39 vs +0.22, no head above 0.2 nats direct so ≥7 heads are forced; 189 heads alone match or beat intact in all three models; flipped-label turn-on across size tracks brakes on word meaning (+1.73→+4.03) not the gate; instruct tuning scales both margin parts by ~2.5 and keeps their ratio. **Limits:** two-class, short sentences, ≤12 demonstrations, ≤8B; minimality genuinely fails; the read-law constants are not separately identifiable and the fixed per-head budgets are unexplained; the duplicate→gate link replicates behaviourally only in Qwen; where brakes come from in training is open.

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 243): **A survival count is not a level but a clock, and the demonstration is the sharpest instance in the folder: one ulp on a millionth of a cache's values — eight orders of magnitude below fp16's distortion — retains 70.5% of features, fp16 itself retains 60.6%, cutting the count of altered scalars from a millionth to 77 barely moves the number (69.9%), and a seed change with no byte changed at all retains 23.0%.** The reading the paper draws is the one to import: the response is flat across six decades of perturbation magnitude and falls only when the quantiser's range is entered (51.2% at 1e-2 relative, on the way to 15.6% for naive int4), so any slope fitted to this curve depends on the window it is fitted over and no single percentage transfers between settings. The companion result is that *matching* criteria are just as brittle: among features a correlation cut counts as matched, the share with the same causal effect on the next-token distribution ranges from 73% down to 16% depending on the condition, per-feature agreement between the two criteria is well short of one, and four partner features recover only about the same fraction of "lost" features in every condition including a pure reseed — which is what licenses the seed change as a unit, because a codec that turns over fewer features than a reseed is causing less of the same thing rather than something else. For our battery: report a floor and a ceiling beside every survival, retention or recovery count, define them in the identical pipeline, and stratify by a stability definition printed in the same sentence, because the level moves with the definition even where the ranking does not. (arxiv-2611.08551, arxiv-2611.01086, arxiv-2611.13548)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 243): **An instrument that is precise and a metric that is informative are independent, and this paper shows three cheap readings of the same cache splitting the two ways: reconstruction error is flat (FVU 0.1355 to 0.1361) across codecs whose feature agreement spans 60.6% to 37.6%, so it cannot register the damage at all; plain distances between caches and the frozen-SAE reading both rank the codecs correctly within a site (Spearman 0.98 and 1.000) yet neither supplies a level, because the same frozen reading of about 0.999 corresponds to 54%, 43% and 38% retained at three sites; and the thresholded frozen reading, which does look like an absolute quantity, inverts one ordering that the continuous reading gets right.** The mechanism behind the middle column is worth keeping as a template: a TopK SAE is piecewise affine, so a codec error either shifts a feature inside its linear region or jumps it across a boundary in or out of the top-k, and a prediction built only from the error's second moment and each feature's margin over the runner-up ranks the per-feature disagreement at a median Spearman of 0.89–0.99 for codecs whose error looks like noise while accounting for the missing damage where a codec removes signal instead (84% of the squared error becomes boundary crossing for naive int4). The generalisable habit is the one the folder keeps re-learning: a metric can be monotone in the treatment and still be unusable as a certification, and the test for which you have is whether its null has been measured — here FVU's null is nonexistent (it never moves) and the frozen reading's null is the wrong kind (a reseed changes no bytes, so it reads 1.000 while only 23% of features survive). (arxiv-2611.08551, arxiv-2611.26004, arxiv-2611.05655)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 243): **When a codec's damage is seeded rather than shared, a multi-seed protocol recovers it and a single-seed one cannot, and the pair of numbers that separates the two regimes is small and decisive: under rotated int8 only 0.13% of seed-stable features are lost in all three seeds against 0.023% expected under independence, while under naive int4 the same figure is 24.16% against 6.876% — so loss is enriched above independence for every codec but is nearly recoverable by re-sampling for the viable ones.** This is the folder's shared-component question in its training-data costume: the same decomposition the aggregation entries apply to per-item error, asked of a perturbation, with the answer deciding whether more seeds are a remedy or a placebo. Two consequences carry over to our own reruns. A treatment we impose on an experiment (a cache format, a decoding rule, a prompt template paraphrased) should be tested for whether its effect is *the same components every time* or *a different sample each time*, because the first will not average out no matter how many seeds are run, and the diagnostic costs no training when paired run files exist. And the budget result says the remedy is training, not storage: as the budget rises from 33M to 328M token-visits the reseed floor climbs from 23.0% to 59.4%, the viable codecs close on the rising floor while naive int4's agreement stays flat, so the fraction of features a *process* finds reliably itself grows with optimisation — which is a reason to report the budget beside any stability figure we quote. (arxiv-2611.08551, arxiv-2611.16315, arxiv-2611.01086)

bf16 forward retains 49.7–51.2 against rot-int8's 51.6–53.8 (2 of 3 seed gaps outside the tie band) at 3072 B/token; 98M-visit equal-bytes tie (32.6% both, 0.02 pp apart) with fresh text giving the same floor (1.09 pp) and the same std-int4 lead; A100 throughput 1.09× local / 1.04× network against a pre-registered 1.15 for material gain; seed-stable losses 0.13% (rot-int8) vs 24.16% (int4); survival predicted from one SAE at AUC 0.868 (all eight measures) and 0.808–0.902 across codecs, with the TopK margin the strongest single statistic and both dictionary-learning predictors (co-firing, decoder coherence) failing; the same change costs 64.7% at step 0 versus 99.9% at step 4,000.

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 242): **An internal pattern can license a claim without establishing it, and this is the sharpest instance in the folder of the two being different acts — the attention heatmaps here suggested two word-theoretic propositions, and the propositions were then proved by hand with braid relations, Matsumoto's theorem and the Weyl action on minimal roots, so the network's contribution was the conjecture and the mathematics' contribution was the result.** The reason this matters for us is that the same composition appears in every entry that reads a pattern as evidence, and it is only legitimate when the second step is available: a proof, a causal intervention, or a held-out prediction. What makes the paper's own use of it disciplined is that it says so — the generative-AI statement records that AI helped with code, figures and literature search but not with proofs or prose — and that the deflationary clause is present too ("likely known by experts"). Two habits follow. Any claim of the form "the model's attention/geometry/feature did X, therefore X is the structure of the task" should carry a statement of what independently establishes it, and if nothing does, the claim is a hypothesis and should be labelled one. And the reverse-direction case is worth noting as a design option: a task with a *known* algorithm is where a proposal can actually be cashed out, which argues for keeping one structured synthetic domain in our battery purely as a place where a white-box model's conjecture is checkable. (arxiv-2611.10936, arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 242): **The cheapest discriminator between a learned procedure and a fitted shortcut is a curve over the variable the procedure must generalise in, and this paper supplies the full two-panel version: accuracy versus word length, plus misclassification rate versus token index.** Trained on unstructured words, test accuracy decayed with length and errors concentrated at the later positions — the signature of something keyed to position statistics rather than to the group's structure — while the same architecture on normal-form words held at no tested length and generalised to subwords never seen in training. The reason to import it is that both panels come free from predictions already made: one extra group-by on length and one on position, no new runs. The related discipline is that the *strict* generalisation test is the unseen-subword count, not the unseen-word count, because a test word can be novel while all its prefixes are not — the paper prints that count explicitly (7,335 unseen subwords on its hardest split) rather than reporting a single accuracy and letting the reader assume. For our own probes this maps onto a habit the folder has only partially adopted: report accuracy stratified by the nuisance the claim says is irrelevant (length, position, difficulty, prefix overlap), because a pooled number is compatible with both a mechanism and a lookup table, and the stratified one usually is not. (arxiv-2611.10936, arxiv-2611.13548, arxiv-2611.09196)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 242): **Masking is a causal test only in its paired form, and the pair here is the cleanest small example in the folder: drop the informative span and accuracy collapses, keep only the informative span and it barely moves, so the first arm alone would have shown merely that the span matters *somewhere* while the second shows it is sufficient.** The asymmetry is what carries the claim — an input region that matters is compatible with redundancy elsewhere, whereas a region that suffices rules out the need for the rest. Two further details make the design copyable. The masking is applied at training as well as test, so the model is not being asked to run off-distribution, which is the usual confound in masking studies. And the masked span is chosen to match a *stated* prediction from the attention pattern rather than picked post hoc, which makes it a test of the interpretation instead of a second look at the data — the same discipline the folder earned about pre-registered thresholds in `arxiv-2611.00606`, arriving on the input side rather than the metric side. (arxiv-2611.10936, arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.11035)
- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 242): `arxiv-2611.10936` — Can small transformers learn the language of Coxeter groups? (J. Elisenda Grigsby, Yiyao Huang, Arushi Katyal, Ryan Lin, Pranav Ramakrishnan, Weiya Wang — Department of Mathematics, Boston College, via the Boston College Experimental Math and Machine Learning Lab; arXiv:2611.10936v1, 2026-11-07, cs.CL (cross-listed cs.LG, math.GR, math.RT), CC BY 4.0, 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted as a poster at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI, NeurIPS 2026 Atlanta). Appendices A–E; **numerals almost entirely stripped by the HTML build**, so no accuracy percentage, dimension or hyperparameter is quoted; figures via captions; the group name recovered from the `/abs/` abstract. **Substance:** a single-layer TransformerLens model (small width, small MLP, no layer norm, biases frozen at zero) trained autoregressively on per-prefix descent-set membership for words in the infinite Coxeter group affine A2, across three datasets of increasing structure — random words (2,000 at length 10), reduced words (2,000 at length 10), and all 1,998 ShortLex normal-form words of length ≤36 at a 30/70 split — plus a keep-only/drop-only masking pair, token-index misclassification breakdowns, and four seeds checking attention-pattern consistency. **Results:** test accuracy decayed with length on the unstructured sets and errors concentrated at later positions, while the ShortLex model held near ceiling at every tested length and generalised to unseen subwords (7,335 unseen on the manual split of 63 words plus random longer words); attention to the final token concentrated on the opening tokens under every seed on the left-descent task and showed a same-parity structure on the right-descent task; masking everything but the first tokens barely moved accuracy while masking the first tokens cost most of it. **Theorems:** (Prop. 1) the right descent set of a minimal-length word lies in its last two letters, always contains the last, and contains the penultimate exactly when a braid-flippable pattern occurs at an odd index; (Prop. 2) the left descent set is determined by the first six letters of the ShortLex normal form — proved via Proposition 3 on odd-index braid-flippable patterns, Casselman's normal-form multiplication and the Weyl action on minimal roots, with a gallery argument covering the even-index and no-index cases. Open: one group, one task, one layer; the Brink–Howlett automaton not exhibited as explicit circuits; the results expected to be known to experts. Tags: unit head, form description, method probing, eval ablation, goal science.

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 241): **An error can be split into a part that is constant for an item across every run and a part that varies between runs, and the ratio decides which question a measurement is answering — here the item-level share is a median 0.906 of the variance, so a team of five has the design-effect-equivalent worth of 1.08 independent draws, teams of thirty buy 1.7% against 74–79% available, and every intervention that perturbs the agents without changing them (debate, temperature, contrastive steering, noise) moves the within-item term and leaves the item term at 2.64 OOM across three rounds.** The methodological payoff is that this is *not* a dependence finding: teammates' residuals correlate at essentially zero given the item and real teams match the resampled-given-the-item reference to within 0.0004 OOM, so the system is perfectly independent and still gains nothing, which separates two questions the folder has been treating as one — "do the members share a mechanism" (residual correlation given the item) from "how much of the error is a per-item constant" (the intraclass component). For our own battery the instrumentation is cheap: any set of repeated measurements per prompt admits a one-way decomposition, and reporting the shared component beside the varying one tells you whether more sampling, more seeds, or a genuinely different intervention is the only thing that can help. The companion design rule is the paired clause in the paper's success criterion — an intervention is credited with reducing the shared error only if it lowers the item component *and* improves the team, because a degraded agent inflates the within-item variance, lowers the ratio, and would otherwise be scored as diversity. (arxiv-2611.16315, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.13548)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 241): **A pooled effect measured under a scheme that randomises the nuisance can vanish without anything about the network changing, and the cleanest demonstration in the folder is that composition, temperature and steering are three different randomisations of the same nuisance with three different answers — mixing five models of similar accuracy gains 6.6% over their own teams and is positive for 99.8% of all 4,928 mixtures, raising temperature to 1.0 gains at most about 1%, and contrastive strategy steering moves the answers by more than the job-to-job variation while changing neither the item component nor team error.** What separates them is not the amount of disagreement created (dispersion rises from 0.100 to 0.438 OOM under temperature, far more than composition) but whether the perturbation is *asymmetric with respect to the error*: an architecture change brings a different single-draw cross-model correlation and therefore a different per-item error sign, whereas temperature and steering resample inside the same model's error distribution. This is the folder's conditioning lesson resolved into an ordering — the denominator of a diversity statistic is the correlation structure, and an intervention that raises variance while preserving the correlation can only change the pooled number through the reference it is normalised against. Two habits follow. Report the reference the diversity gain is measured against *in the same table* as the gain, since a 6.6% improvement and a 1% improvement here are the same statistic against different baselines. And never credit a mechanism claim to an intervention that leaves the item-level component unchanged, because that component is where a per-item mechanism would show up. (arxiv-2611.16315, arxiv-2611.13548, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 241): **An instrument that removes the part of the error you can see need not touch the part that survives, and two arms here fail in exactly that shape: a cross-validated linear recalibration from estimate to truth removes the overall bias (item component changing by a median −0.4%) while leaving the compression intact, since the fitted slope is below one and a map whose only input is the estimate cannot separate item-specific error from true magnitude; and calculator offload, which removes the arithmetic step, makes the team significantly worse with catastrophic answers rising from 51.5% to 66.9%.** Both are the folder's recurring "the metric moved, the mechanism did not" failure arriving with a variance decomposition attached, and the second supplies the diagnosis: the instrument was pointed at the wrong stage, because an unconstrained product of several wrong factors is less bounded than one wrong intuition, so removing the multiplication only lets a bad factor choice propagate. The general rule worth importing is that an intervention should be aimed at the component the decomposition says is dominant, not at the component that is easiest to instrument — and where the two differ, the intervention's failure is *evidence about the decomposition*, not a null result about the intervention. The paired detail is that the two arms which did lower the item component are the two the paper declines to endorse, one for failing Holm correction across six prompt arms and one for resting on a single-model 150-item screen with the earlier parser; a result that points the right way and is not powered to establish it is reported as a candidate, which is the disposition our own screening runs should copy. (arxiv-2611.16315, arxiv-2611.11035, arxiv-2611.04349)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 240): **A patching result is ambiguous until the donor is varied along at least three axes, and this paper's four-way panel is the ladder to copy — the same instance's state (content, if anything carries it), a deranged state from another instance (no content), the norm-rescaled mean (content-free *and* instance-independent), and the HIGH-minus-LOW mean difference added to the subject's own state (content-free and linear) — and the reading that follows is that a layer where all four jump together is supplying a default, not a payload.** The panel earns its place twice over. It produces a *positive* test for a content channel rather than only a null: the wrong-segment donor becomes actively **worse** than the unpatched run at the layers where matched separates, so harm from the shuffled donor is the signature that a content channel has opened, and a design that only compared matched against clean could never see it. And the additive donor separates a direction question from a state question: because mean_diff preserves the instance's own vector and still reproduces the effect, the content-free signal is a single additive direction rather than an overwrite, which is exactly the distinction our own steering-versus-patching comparisons need. Scaling the mean donor back to the average per-instance norm is the detail that makes the null interpretable, because otherwise "the mean donor did nothing" is confounded with "the mean donor is small". Three habits for our battery: build the donor set from the *same matched instance first* and let the controls vary one property at a time; report a shuffled-donor penalty beside the matched gain at every depth, since the two curves cross at the interesting layer; and treat a norm-rescaled mean as the null for any claim of the form "the donor supplied information about *this* input". (arxiv-2611.12538, arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.18089)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 240): **Sparse representability and causal effectiveness are independent, and the cleanest evidence is a *dip* rather than a null: the span of the effective direction by its top dictionary vectors is high early, falls exactly at the layers where the direction is causal, and recovers after — and doubling the feature budget barely moves the dipped value — while a dictionary rebuilt from the same features cannot reproduce the effect at any width or steering strength, and the converse case shows a direction the dictionary spans well and no feature of which changes behaviour.** This is the folder's dictionary-miss lesson arriving with a measurement instead of a warning: the earlier form was "reconstruction error hides what the dictionary lacks", which is a caveat, whereas a dip in explained span localised to the causal layers says the model's effective direction is *distributed* precisely where it matters, which is a falsifiable claim about the network. Two consequences follow. Any sentence of the form "the dictionary recovered direction X, therefore X is the mechanism" is unsupported even when the span is one, because span is measured by least squares against decoder vectors and not by intervention — report both, and report the span *per layer* rather than pooled, since pooling would average the dip away. And the negative arm needs a fidelity number in the same sentence: this paper's three dictionary families give an interpretable split at the highest fidelity, a de-noised vector dominated by reconstruction error at the middle one, and no usable analysis at the lowest, where the authors decline to run the test — which is the right way to report an instrument that runs out of resolution rather than a result (arxiv-2611.12538, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2610.30474)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 240): **When a direction is carried by a *set* of features, the control that makes removal interpretable is an equal-mass random removal, and the pair of them decides whether the effect is about identity or about quantity — here stripping an instance's own feature mass from the donor helps at the flip layer and then hurts progressively at later layers, renormalising the shrunken vector changes nothing at any layer, and removing the same mass from a random equal-count set of the instance's active features is far worse throughout.** The three-arm design is worth importing whole because each arm kills one explanation: the random arm kills "any perturbation of this size would do", the renormalisation arm kills "the effect is just a smaller vector", and the depth reversal is the finding — the same subtraction is helpful and harmful at different depths, so the *content* of the removed features has a sign that changes with the layer. This is the same shape as the folder's earlier content-matched controls, but reversed in direction of reasoning: those held the contrast and varied the match, while this one holds the match and varies the *attribution* of the removed mass to the instance. It also supplies a caution the paper states against itself: its own explanation of a late-layer anomaly (instance-specific content competing with the model's encoding) predicted that the subtraction would move matched *toward* the mean donor, and it moved sharply away — so an explanation that suggests a cheap confirming experiment should be run, because here the experiment refuted it and the alternative metric had already failed to reproduce the anomaly. (arxiv-2611.12538, arxiv-2611.18089, arxiv-2611.09196)

Full text, 81,243 raw chars incl. Appendices A–F and the logit-lens appendix; **inline numerals stripped throughout by the HTML build**, so every per-layer chrF++, flip fraction, cumulative-R² value and Qwen/Llama difference cell is described as a direction of effect rather than quoted; Table 1's onset layers and the appendix pair counts survived as cells; figures via captions. **Substance:** success–failure contrasts on multi-parallel FLORES+/NTREX and Belebele, patching one last-token residual vector at one layer, with a four-donor panel (matched / seeded shuffled / norm-rescaled mean / additive mean_diff) and pairs grouped into same-target, different-target-same-source and disjoint; three pretrained models (gemma-3-4b-pt primary, Qwen3.5-9B-Base and Llama-3.1-8B replicated), three SAE families (Gemma Scope 2 JumpReLU, Qwen-Scope and Llama-Scope TopK), sparse interventions tested as add / ablate / both at two widths and two strengths. **Results:** three stages with onset layers L16/18/13, L17/19/14 and L24/28/24 (Gemma/Qwen/Llama) — English default content-independent (all four donors rise together, matched−shuffled null, median onset consistent across conditions, Latin-script mass stepping up at the same layers in the logit lens), content onset one layer later (matched separates and stays separated to the last layer, shuffled becomes worse than clean on same-target pairs, Belebele lifts off chance and reproduces the HIGH pass's own answer at the same layer, task-independent), specific target late and only for non-English (sister pairs later with near-zero flip fraction, cross-script between, Kashmiri an exception where every donor switches together). **Dissociation both ways:** span of the flip direction by its top decoder vectors dips at exactly the causal layers and doubling the feature budget barely helps; no sparse intervention flips any English-target pair at either width or strength while all dense donors do; conversely the sister-language direction is well spanned and no feature flips it. De-noised donor: helps at the flip layer, hurts progressively after, renormalisation null, random equal-mass removal far worse. **Fidelity bounds the instrument** — interpretable on Gemma, reconstruction-dominated on Qwen, refused on Llama — while the patching account transfers to all three. Limits: single position, single layer, one vector at a time (availability, not localisation of the computation); xCOMET-selected instances; the same position restriction applies to the sparse negatives, which the paper does not restate there.

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 239): **An intervention can reduce the behaviour it targets and the behaviour you wanted at once, and the only way to see it is to score the two outcomes on the same items — here the layer-18 "keep" direction removes caving entirely (6.1% to 0.0%) while nearly removing self-correction (13.8% to 1.5%), leaving accuracy exactly where it started, and every variant of the direction (shared component removed, the change-when-wrong direction added, a same-norm random vector at a fixed ~0.6 ratio) stays on one caving–correction frontier.** This is the folder's selectivity lesson with a mechanism attached: when both outcomes are produced by the same internal quantity, a one-dimensional intervention cannot trade between them, so the frontier *is* the evidence that the quantity is shared — the paper reads its own steering results as a diagnostic of the representation, not as a control result. Three habits follow for our battery. Any edit we publish is scored on the complement outcome as well as the target one, because a direction that only appears to work by freezing the model will pass a single-outcome test. A random-direction control is not sufficient on its own when it lands on the *same frontier*, since that is what shows the frontier is a property of the model rather than of the direction — the dissociation the paper actually finds is between prefilled and free replies, not between real and random directions. And the gated-steering number is the honest ceiling on this whole style of control: predicting *where* the intervention is safe (AUROC 0.81) recovers 0.4 and 1.0 points of an oracle's 6.9 and 1.5, so the gate is the binding constraint long before the direction is. (arxiv-2611.11035, arxiv-2611.04349, arxiv-2611.18089)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 239): **The unit of comparison can make an effect change sign, and here the unit is a token budget — the same questions, the same models and the same pre-reply hidden states give "pushback hurts accuracy" at 96 tokens and "pushback helps by 5.7 points" at 1,024, because the short run truncates 83% of replies so self-correction never gets to happen, and correction rises 6–31 points with full replies while the cave rate moves only a few.** Because the recorded states do not depend on the budget, the entire difference is in what the model does *while* replying, which turns a generation-length knob into a variable about the computation and not about the experiment. This is the folder's conditioning lesson arriving in its most mundane costume: the earlier instances were an answer letter, a prompt-pooled denominator and a sequence mean, and this one is the number of tokens the model may spend, which no steering paper we have read prints. The paired-size discipline is the transferable part: run both arms on identical items, report the truncation rate beside each outcome, and treat a truncated subsample as its own diagnostic — here truncated Qwen 4B replies caved 38.7% against 12.4% for complete ones, so truncation is not noise but a variable correlated with the outcome. And the budget also decides whether a *representation* claim holds: the probe-transfer evidence for a shared caving/correction signal is present under truncation in all three models and vanishes under full replies. (arxiv-2611.11035, arxiv-2611.13548, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 239): **A cosine between two mean-difference directions is close to uninformative inside a residual stream, and the paper proves it on its own claim — the caving and correcting directions agreed at 0.785, but the same cosine computed after shuffling the labels reached 0.6–0.9 even after z-scoring, and the sign of the raw value flipped between two runs that differed only in their labels, so the measurement was withdrawn and replaced by a transfer test whose chance level is exactly 0.5 by construction.** The lesson is not "cosines are bad" but "the null must be computed in the same geometry", which is sharper than the folder's existing shuffle controls: run 232's within-sequence shuffle and run 231's self-comparison diagonal both hold a quantity fixed and ask how much of the score survives, whereas a label shuffle here reveals that the *statistic's null* is nowhere near zero, so the 0.785 was never evidence of anything. The remedy costs one retrain and is architecture-independent: any statement of the form "these two internal signals are the same" is tested by training a predictor on one group and scoring it on the other against a strong baseline, with paired-bootstrap intervals, and is never supported by a similarity score whose null has not been measured. The companion result sets the ceiling on that stronger test too — the probe alone never significantly beats turn-1 confidence anywhere in this paper, and the information it supplies is only additive (0.04–0.06 AUROC, from 0.747 to 0.804), so a small but real gain over a cheap baseline is the realistic size of what residual-stream probes contribute to a behavioural prediction. (arxiv-2611.11035, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.18089)

Full text, 24,012 raw chars (the shortest in recent runs: 10 pages, no appendices); Table 1 and Table 2 populated as grids and quoted as cells; inline math stripped, so equation (1), the break-even formula and a few prose ranges render blank and are reconstructed from their prose statements or filled from table cells; figures 1–5 via captions only. **Substance:** a four-option question, a logit-read answer, an uninformative challenge, a free reply of up to a budget, and a logit-read final answer, classifying every question into cave/correction/hold and comparing budgets on identical items; four models (Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B, OLMo-2-7B) in 4-bit on one GPU, MMLU and ARC-Challenge. **Results:** the accounting identity (1−a)·r − a·c gives a break-even accuracy r/(r+c); budget reverses the verdict (Qwen 4B MMLU −1.3 at 96 tokens to +5.7 at 1,024, cave 8.4→13.6, correction 12.3→43.2; Qwen 8B −2.6→+3.8; Qwen 4B ARC −0.1→+3.9 at a fixed 3.6% cave rate; correction up 6–31 points across paired settings); truncation correlates with caving (38.7% against 12.4%); break-even explains OLMo's negative ARC setting (74.2% below 76.6%); a stacked hidden-state probe lifts AUROC over confidence 0.747→0.804 and 0.797→0.841 (Qwen 4B) and 0.754→0.806 (OLMo), never alone significantly, with 11.3%/12.8% of high-confidence right answers still abandoned; probe transfer from wrong-answer to right-answer cases at 0.57–0.69 AUROC and positive gain under truncation in all three tested models, indistinguishable from zero under full replies; steering removes caving and correction together on one frontier, random directions move both at ~0.6, gated steering recovers 0.4/1.0 against an oracle's 6.9/1.5; the cosine-similarity evidence (0.785) is withdrawn in favour of the transfer test after shuffle controls reached 0.6–0.9. Limits: ≤8B 4-bit, one challenge wording, MCQ only, cost-driven prefilled-reply screening, small OLMo long-reply run.

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 238): **The two intervention settings this folder has compared for 238 entries — one direction for everything, versus a direction recomputed per example — are endpoints of a single family, and the parameter that walks between them is a neighbourhood size, so "fixed versus per-example" was never a binary choice but a choice of locality: the retrieved mean of the k nearest stored targets inside the requested class is the class-conditional class mean at k equal to the class size, word-level edits select a few neighbours at the embedding layer and loosen with depth, clause-level edits sit at the class mean until deep in the stack, and replacing the selected k with the class ceiling costs most of the margin on the corpora that are local.** This matters because run 236's headline was 8/8 seeds passing under per-pair directions and 0/8 under fitted-once ones, and the natural reading — that the per-example setting is the only one that works — is now too coarse: the intermediate rung is available from exactly the labels the fixed rule already requires (no aligned pairs), and the paper's coverage experiment shows what happens when it cannot be used (degradation to the class-conditional mean, not arbitrary failure). For our battery this converts a comparison into a *sweep with a stated meaning*: report the selected locality, because it tells you which rule won, and report coverage, because the margin is largely a coverage effect. The paired lesson is about depth: the level of the concept being edited — a word or a whole clause — sets where in the network the edit should be applied far more cleanly than it sets how good the edit can be, which is the folder's recurring "depth is the hidden parameter" finding arriving with an operational rule attached. (arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.04349, arxiv-2611.14168)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 238): **A corpus can make a metric structurally unable to register what a rule does, and here the construction is so simple it is worth copying as a template: one concept rendered in one frame with only its destination span differing across classes gives every query the same source state, so any rule that is a function of the source state alone maps all of them to one steered state, and one point can be nearest to at most one of their references — per-item identity is therefore capped at the reciprocal of the class count by construction rather than by estimation error.** The authors prove this from their own corpus design, show the most-supervised fixed rule (a fitted affine map) hitting the cap exactly on the control corpus, and then use it as the test that separates reading the requested class from not reading it; the fixed mean and the affine map both sit at or below the cap on every corpus, while retrieval clears it on five of six. The generalisable habit is to ask, of every metric we report, whether some class of method is barred from passing it *by the data rather than by its quality*, and to print that bar next to the score: the folder has met degenerate ceilings before (the saturated probe at 0.998, the faithfulness reward above the task threshold, the f1.0 on a rare class) but always as a property of the *score's* range, never as a property of the *query set*. Two companion metrics show how to pair it — reference error normalised by the corpus's mean required step so that doing nothing reads near one, and a class-balanced forced choice so a rule with a fixed preference for one class scores exactly chance — and the second is the same discipline as run-237's endpoint enrichment, applied to a probe set instead of a feature stratum. (arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.05655)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 238): **A pooled task statistic can be wrong in sign because a nuisance variable cancels the signal, and the fix is to print the conditioned value beside the pooled one and call the gap itself the diagnostic — here the "shared fraction" of the required edit reads near zero on two A/B benchmarks, which is the signature of required edits that disagree, while computed within a fixed answer letter it rises to almost one, because the items' two states differ mainly in which option is selected and those flips cancel when pooled.** The paper draws the correct conclusion from its own reversal: the pooled quantity looks like input-dependence and is a formatting artefact, so a quantity whose sign depends on which comparison is being made must never be screened on alone, and where a nuisance factor is known in advance, report both. The positive counterpart is that the diagnostic computed on *the search the rule actually performs* — agreement between the optimally retrieved displacement and the true one — is not fooled, which is why it ranks the retrieval rule's own error best and why the paper trusts it wherever a bank exists. For our battery this is the denominator lesson in its third costume (after a metric's denominator in run 230 and a baseline's drift in run 233): a statistic can be correct arithmetic on the wrong conditioning set, and the diagnosis is cheap because the conditioned version is one extra group-by. It also gives a usable scale rule — the paper's diagnostics say *whether* input-dependent steering can help but none of them ranks *how much*, and the one that ranks the outcome best needs a bank and hundreds of pairs while the residual needs a handful, so the screening budget decides which diagnostic is affordable before the experiment decides which is best. (arxiv-2611.04757, arxiv-2611.13548, arxiv-2611.08438)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 237): **A pooled semantic score over a dictionary is a mixture of a dominant head and a long tail that behave oppositely, and this paper measures the head for the first time — the top dominance quartile scores 61.8% perfect-ranking accuracy against 64.1% for the rest, 65.2% of 600+ SAEs show the deficit individually, and even in dictionaries of 4,000–128,000 features the ten most frequently firing features carry a median 7.8% of per-input activation.** The structural point is that uniform aggregation across features is not a neutral default but an *implicit choice of denominator*, and it is the wrong one whenever usage is skewed, which it always is: a misinterpreted dominant feature distorts a large share of what the dictionary says about the input, while a misinterpreted tail feature distorts almost nothing. This is the run-231 lesson with its sign flipped and both ends now measured — there the *low*-energy tail carried most of the between-seed instability while the top-50 audit showed a stable head; here the head is where the polysemanticity and the redundancy are. The two together are the strongest case in the folder for never reporting a dictionary-level scalar without a stratification, because each end fails a different criterion and a pooled number can be held up either way. Operationally: pick the stratifier by the claim being made — energy or dominance if the claim is about what the dictionary says on a given input, seed-variance if it is about whether the dictionary would come back the same way — and print the stratum's own population rate beside it (this paper's *endpoint enrichment* is exactly that normalisation, quartile share of bad edges divided by quartile share of active features). (arxiv-2610.30474, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.13548)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 237): **A binary validation label can make a scoring rule unable to fail, and the fix is to make the label an ordering — the failure is structural, not statistical: if a feature fires on two unrelated rare triggers, a uniformly sampled validation set contains neither, every explanation correctly predicts "does not fire", and a confidently wrong description scores perfectly; the same happens at the other end for near-always-on features, where no negative is samplable.** Their replacement asks a judge to rank three held-out examples drawn from own-quantile low/medium/high bins with the activation values hidden, and scores exact orderings, which cannot be passed by predicting one class; on 80 synthetic features with generator-fixed truth it orders correctly for all 80 where a discretised-magnitude rule manages 67 and binary and fuzz-style rules at most 22, on the same explanations and the same held-out evidence. Two things generalise. Any of our own probes that we validate by classification inherit this hole whenever the positive rate is extreme, and the tell is a score at exactly 1.0 on a rare class — the same *ceiling* signature the folder has met in the saturated-probe and same-model-preference entries, arriving from the sampling side rather than the model side. And the rank-versus-threshold distinction is worth keeping in the metric vocabulary: a threshold statistic compresses a continuous difference into a pass/fail and can be satisfied by a degenerate constant, whereas a ranking statistic over a matched triple has to discriminate. Cheapest version for us: sample the validation triple from the feature's *own* quantiles rather than the corpus's, since corpus sampling is what makes both extremes unsamplable. (arxiv-2610.30474, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.08438)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 237): **Two features can be the same direction and different concepts at once, and the fingerprint is decoder-aligned, encoder-orthogonal, support-complementary — a TopK-65k Pythia-160M pair with decoder cosine 0.7405 and encoder cosine 0.2066 fires 316 times and 57 times with 7 co-firings (Jaccard 0.019), one keyed to definite articles and one to possessives, and injecting both at positions where neither gate fires natively moves the same target logit with effect vectors at cosine 0.943.** The mechanism is a training incentive rather than a bug: sharding satisfies sparsity (only one shard fires per input), satisfies reconstruction (the same direction is written either way) and reduces dead features (each shard owns a slice of context), so the dictionary looks healthy under every standard diagnostic while its effective semantic dictionary is several times smaller than its width. This is a **third** distinct failure from the two the folder already knows — absorption has one support nested inside another (15.3% of decoder-aligned pairs here), sharding has them largely disjoint (21.5%) — so no single redundancy or absorption check catches both, and a decoder-cosine test alone will flag shards as duplicates when the right reading is one concept split by context. For our reading of weights: the three columns to print for any feature pair we call "the same feature" or "a duplicate" are decoder cosine, encoder cosine and support overlap, in that order; and for any intervention claim, two similar decoder writes are evidence of a shared direction, not of a shared role, which is the same caution the folder earned about identical directions steering different behaviours. (arxiv-2610.30474, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.14168)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 236): **A steering result's strongest claim can be an artefact of information the deployed system would not have, and this paper makes that a declared factor instead of a caveat — the same supports, the same panels and the same budget score 8/8 seeds passing under directions recomputed from each evaluation pair and 0/8 under directions averaged over the fitting split, on both head-level multiple choice (0.169–0.192 against 1.010–1.031) and sentiment (0.167–0.171 against 0.742–0.746), with feedback endpoints falling from 45–47 of 48 to 7–8 of 48 and reversal counts from 21–23 of 24 to 0 of 24.** The 0/8-versus-8/8 shape is worth internalising because it is not a partial degradation: a fixed direction is not a slightly worse controller, it is a controller that never reaches the tolerance, and the monotone quantities still move (the dose curves remain ordered, some strongly so) while the thresholded ones do not — which is exactly why a dosage sweep alone would have reported success. Two habits follow for our battery. Declare the direction-information condition of every steering claim at the level of what the method reads at deployment: per-example contrast, fitted-once mean, probe normal, or SAE decoder — and never compare a per-example result against a fitted-once baseline as if the difference were about selection quality. And read the paper's own honesty about this as the model to copy: it puts the restriction in the conclusion and the limitations section, and it names the cost of its own positive result rather than the difficulty of its negative one. (arxiv-2611.04349, arxiv-2610.31520, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 236): **Monotone dose response and reversibility are independent properties, and the cleanest dissociation in the folder is an intervention that is perfectly ordered and never inverts — all 48 refusal dose curves have a rank correlation of exactly 1 with dose while none of 24 method–seed cells passes target-side reversal in either direction condition, so the same support walks the readout in one direction and cannot walk it back.** The mechanism the numbers point at is that a dose multiplier scales a fixed displacement, so any intervention whose effect is linear in dose will look perfectly ordered whenever the readout moves at all, and ordering therefore tests almost nothing beyond "the patch does something consistent"; reversal tests whether the patch is a *signed* quantity whose negation is also a valid intervention, which is a different structural property and one a truncation or a one-sided feature cannot satisfy. The generalisation is direct for our own edits: a monotone dose curve is a weak evidence class, and the two strong classes are the negated-patch return and the off-target panel, which here fail almost everywhere (no seed meets either the mean or the all-prompt 0.001-KL criterion on three tasks under any selector, mean KL 0.110–0.582). So the folder's many "steering scales with coefficient" observations should be read as consistency checks and never as evidence of control, and any intervention we publish should carry the negated patch and a preservation panel beside it, because those are the two that can fail. (arxiv-2611.04349, arxiv-2610.31520, arxiv-2611.08438)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 236): **The cheapest and most decisive test of whether a finding is about a location or about a fitted artefact is to keep the site and refit the coefficients — recovery goes from 0.992 ± 0.009 and 0.987 ± 0.034 with the sites retained to 0.021 ± 0.026 and 0.024 ± 0.066 with the whole intervention frozen, a factor of roughly forty, on identical supports, identical held-out questions and identical direction rules.** Because both arms read the same sites, nothing about localisation changes across the comparison; the only thing removed is the fitting, so the gap measures how much of the effect was carried by coefficients tuned on the evaluation-side targets and by directions computed per prompt. The paper's phrasing of the conclusion is the precise one to borrow: reusable sites do not imply transferable interventions, and the two belong in separate sentences with separate numbers. Two further points sharpen it. The refit arm still has access to held-out targets, so 0.99 is an upper bound on site reuse rather than a transfer claim, and the fully frozen arm's near-zero is the number that corresponds to what deployment would actually ship. And the same distinction recurs inside the feedback axis, where a fixed support tracks 46 of 48 endpoints by adjusting only its dose and 8 of 48 once the directions are also frozen — so "the support generalises" and "the controller generalises" are again two statements. For our battery: every claim of the form "we found the site/direction/feature that does X" should ship with both arms, because the frozen arm is the only one a practitioner can run without the targets. (arxiv-2611.04349, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.18089)

- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 235): **A dictionary has two numbers that can disagree about the same dictionary, and the folder has only ever reported one of them — fidelity says how much of the representation the atoms carry, stability says how far the decomposition is *unique*, and here the two order the candidate units in opposite directions: neurons are at maximum fidelity by construction and fail stability, released dictionary features buy stability with fidelity, and neither class reaches both criteria in any of the three model families at either dictionary width.** The stability half is the part to steal: it is the largest quantile q at which the empirical sparsity level k and the maximum coherence μ satisfy kμ below the uniqueness threshold, found by bisection, so it returns a fraction of the data on which the guarantee holds rather than a yes/no verdict — a sparse decomposition on the other fraction is one of several equally good explanations and no amount of fidelity evidence selects among them. Two design details make it attackable rather than decorative. The inner product is *chosen*, not inherited: the authors replace the Euclidean metric with one induced by the representations' own second-order statistics, argue it is the only one invariant under the invertible reparameterisations that leave the network's function untouched, and then show the choice is load-bearing — under the Euclidean cosine, pairs of unrelated entities sit systematically away from 90° in every layer of GPT-2-Large, Pythia-6.9B and Llama-3.1-8B, the shift does not shrink with the sample size, and the corrected metric recentres the distributions while leaving the high-similarity tail intact. That is the dominant-direction artefact the folder has met as a fidelity problem (PC1 owning the variance) and as a denominator problem, here arriving as a **geometry** problem: coherence, cosine and orthogonality are metric-dependent quantities, and a superposition or orthogonality claim quoted in the ambient metric is partly a claim about the basis. And the criterion has a known failure mode the paper half-admits: stability can always be raised by shrinking the dictionary, which is why the HowNet arm fixes width per model and the sweep reports eight combinations rather than one. For our battery: print (R², uniqueness quantile) as a pair, state the metric, and check the metric's own angular centroid before any coherence number. (arxiv-2611.14168, arxiv-2611.13548, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.00606)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 235): **A structural guarantee and a semantic one are different objects, and the discipline of keeping them apart — proving the first, measuring the second, and printing the correlation that links them — is the cleanest form of claim this folder has seen from a dictionary paper: the theorem here gives monorepresentationality (each sparse decomposition is unique), the experiments give monosemanticity (a unit's activations admit one specific interpretation), and the paper states plainly that the first is necessary for the second and demonstrably not sufficient, then reports a positive rank correlation between a dictionary's stability and a judge-scored monosemanticity across 40 dataset–model–SAE combinations, within each corpus and within all eight model settings.** Everything that makes this honest is in what it does not do: it never lets the theorem stand in for the measurement, it names the sufficiency gap rather than arguing it away, and its judge protocol is restricted so the cheapest failure mode cannot fire — the shared interpretation must be specific, so "all of these are entities" or "all are words" does not count, and a manual pass revises the judge where its boundary is too broad. The complementary result is the ceiling it puts on the whole enterprise: **about one percent of hand-annotated human concepts are recovered by a single atom, and most take more than six atoms across layers** (DISTRICT needs 49 atoms at F1 0.983 in Gemma-2-2B, DAY 166 at 0.894, CAPITAL 126 at 0.992), with F1 rising as the greedy combination grows and sememe complexity predicting the atom count in a log–log fit. The direct consequence is stated in the paper's own discussion of editing and steering and is worth carrying into our intervention work: if a human concept is a cross-layer composition, then an edit aimed at one direction touches part of a concept or several at once, which is the mechanical story behind incomplete edits and collateral effects. And the control that makes the compositional claim survivable is an **equivalence** test — cross-layer width versus F1, bounded to a prespecified |r| — because a greedy search over a larger pool will always look better and a null-hypothesis test on that correlation would have licensed the artefact. (arxiv-2611.14168, arxiv-2611.08438, arxiv-2611.09196, arxiv-2611.13548)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 235): **When the reference ontology itself is wrong in both directions, the residual of a semantic alignment is evidence rather than error, and this paper is the rare one that audits the difference set instead of reporting the score — the entities a combination recovers but HowNet does not annotate include a Bavarian restaurant brand and Red Square under DISTRICT for Llama-3.1-8B and a hyperthermophile genus under BACTERIA for Gemma-2-2B, while the entities HowNet does annotate include an announcer and game theory under BACTERIA and the bare word "district" in one Gemma-2-9B difference set, and both classes were found by hand and marked in the table.** The methodological point generalises past this paper: any set-matching score against a human-authored gold standard is a measurement of two objects at once, so a low F1 has two indistinguishable explanations and the only way to separate them is to read a sample of the disagreements — the cost here was one table with two marked columns. The companion caution is that the audit cuts the claim both ways: if part of the mismatch is annotation error, part of it may also be the model's own coherent-but-not-human organisation, and the paper says so rather than counting every unannotated hit as a discovery. Two habits follow. Any benchmark score we report against a curated resource ships with a marked sample of both difference sets, because the mismatches are where the information about the instrument lives. And where the resource is small and hand-made (2,135 sememes here after dropping those with fewer than two entities), report the filter itself — the restriction to two-or-more-entity sememes silently excludes the whole tail of rare concepts, which is exactly the tail where a dictionary's atom-per-concept resolution would be hardest to establish. (arxiv-2611.14168, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.09196)
- Done 2026-11-16 (entry 235): `arxiv-2611.14168` — Representational Atoms in Neural Networks (Chenhui Hu, Pengfei Cao, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao; Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences + UCAS; arXiv:2611.14168v1, 2026-11-10, arXiv perpetual non-exclusive licence, code at github.com/ChenhuiHu/representational_atoms). Full text, 140,488 raw chars incl. the Methods, Extended Data Figs. 1–5, Tables 1–5 and the Supplementary Information proofs; figures via captions; inline math and the numeric bodies of Tables 1 and Extended Data Tables 1–4 blanked by the HTML build, so the paper's headline fidelity/stability cells and all correlation coefficients are described rather than quoted. **Substance:** define a fundamental representational unit as a dictionary whose representations are sparse combinations of unit-norm atoms, with **fidelity** (R² of reconstruction) and **stability** (the largest quantile at which the empirical sparsity × coherence product still satisfies the classical coherence uniqueness condition, computed by bisection under a representation-induced "atomic inner product"), then compare candidate units on both. - Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 234): **A first-order graph's error is set by the read-out rule, not by the derivative, and the fix costs nothing because the columns are already computed — a TopK dictionary is a selection over all preactivations, so the support the attribution graph is built on is exactly the set an intervention perturbs: zeroing one feature moves a downstream feature across the cutoff in 0.74–0.92 of cases, the crossing coordinates carry 0.73–0.84 of the response's energy, and re-applying the rule to the first-order-predicted preactivations drops the median relative error from 0.247–0.669 to 0.013–0.033, with the reranking alone worth the whole improvement because removing it returns the error to 0.558.** The general statement is stronger than the TopK case and is what makes this entry portable: any read-out that *selects* — TopK, a threshold, an argmax over heads, a router's top-2, a renormalised attention pattern — is discontinuous in its input, so a first-order expansion taken at the clean point is evaluated on a membership that the expansion itself predicts will change. The recipe is one line: keep every row of the Jacobian-vector product, add it to all preactivations, and re-run the rule. Two design notes from the paper's own ablation are worth copying. The measured quantity has to be the *code* change and not the preactivation change, because a leaver's code drops from at least the cutoff to zero and an entrant's jumps from zero to near it, so a crossing coordinate's code moves 5.7–10.1 times as far as its preactivation while the preactivation error stays small for both — an error metric on the smooth quantity cannot see the discontinuity. And the contrast that makes the discontinuity attributable is a ReLU dictionary on the same model family, which crosses its zero just as often (0.69) and carries almost none of the response (0.05 of the energy) precisely because its code is continuous there; a crossing rate without a continuous-rule control would read as a fact about dictionaries rather than about the rule that selects. (arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.09233, arxiv-2611.08438)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 234): **The cheapest discipline in the folder is to write each prediction down with the threshold at which it fails before the measurement, print what came back beside it, and let the ones that fire against you stay — 22 rules here, six fired, and three of the six are adverse to the paper's own headline: the once-built graph loses to the plain fixed-support graph on sixteen-feature subsets (0.670 against 0.631), a two-layer MLP given exactly the margin graph's six inputs fails to reach it (2.23–2.45 error, and 1.44–1.53 on two inputs, both worse than predicting no change at 1.0, against 0.016), and the residual chain passes where the decoded chains fail.** Table 1's four columns — what the rule reads, when it fires, what the measurement returned, and whether it fired — is a better artefact than a limitations section because it is a ledger a reader can audit line by line, and because it makes the boundary of a claim a number instead of an adjective: the margin graph is licensed at the median write (1.68 and 3.57 cutoff units) and not at the write where the first-order error reaches 0.3 (5.55 and 3.90), and the paper says both. Two habits follow for our battery. Every metric we report should arrive with a pre-registered kill threshold, because the alternative is choosing the threshold after seeing the number, which is how a battery of 40 tests ends up with 40 passes. And the against-the-headline firings are the ones to keep visible: a paper that only published the fired rules favouring it would be indistinguishable from one that chose its thresholds afterwards, and the tell that it did not is precisely that some of its own predictions misfire. (arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.08438, arxiv-2611.05655)
- Pattern 2026-11-16 (run 234): **A decoded per-feature response and the model's own activation change are two different quantities with opposite-looking statistics, and reporting both is the only way to see it — over crossing interventions the part of the decoded code change on entering and leaving features has 1.24–1.72 times the activation change's norm while projecting at only 0.21–0.29 of it, the whole decoded change has 1.41–1.82 times the norm at a median cosine of 0.27–0.50, and the reconstruction residual supplies the difference, so the dictionary's response is both larger than and badly aligned with the thing it is supposed to describe.** The downstream consequence is the sharpest result in the paper and the one to carry: carrying a *decoded middle code* through the next block fails at the third layer (0.884 for the fixed-support chain, 0.999 and 0.996 for the margin and exact ones), while carrying the *residual stream* through both blocks in one product per live feature errs 0.053 and the exact activation-change chain 0.029 — the decoded code is not the object that composes across layers, and the reconstruction error it drops is a real part of the model's forward pass. For our own multi-hop claims this is a concrete test that costs two extra products: compare a chain built from codes against a chain built from activations, at the third layer's code. The paired lesson is about stability scores: per-feature cosine matching leaves the operator between two layers at 0.22 explained, where sparse non-negative recombinations of atoms reach 0.57, and the whole remaining gap sits on the target's atoms nearest the cutoff (admitting 10% of them nearest-first recovers 0.73 of it, a random 10% only 0.11) — so "the features agree across seeds" and "the graph agrees across seeds" are measurements of different objects, and the operator, not the feature direction, is the one that decides whether a circuit claim survives a change of seed. (arxiv-2611.00606, arxiv-2611.05655, arxiv-2611.18089)

Margin graph 0.013–0.033 against 0.247–0.669 (testbed 0.017 against 0.786), difference above zero on every pair by a 2,000-draw bootstrap over positions; reranking removed → 0.558; entering-set precision 0.80–0.90 / recall 0.82–0.92, and 0.84–0.93 at the true entrant count against 0.42–0.49 for margin alone. Once-built graph: 0.287 vs 0.770 at subsets of two, 0.458 vs 0.551 at sixteen, and worse than the fixed support on the release at sixteen (0.670 vs 0.631). First-order error reaches 0.3 at writes of 5.55 and 3.90 cutoff units (boundaries 7.26 and 4.36 pooled, ratio 1.66 under a 2.0 pre-registration) against median writes of 1.68 and 3.57; the band accepts 0.59–0.87 of single-write memberships (coverage 0.21–0.71 at zero dose, 0.97–1.00 at 0.9) and 0.012–0.067 of subset writes, with no wrong membership among 668,393,327. Readout: entering-and-leaving norm 1.24–1.72× (testbed 1.56), projection share 0.21–0.29, whole decoded change 1.41–1.82× at cosine 0.27–0.50; decoded middle chains 0.884 / 0.999 / 0.996 at the third layer against 0.029 exact and 0.053 residual. Transport: 0.57 unmasked vs 0.22 one-to-one (gain 0.35 over a 0.19 bound, 30 of 30 pairs beating 20 random and 200 null draws at one product), 0.47 masked, 0.85 with the whole target dictionary, gap 0.38 = 0.34 mask energy + 0.05 cross term; nearest-cutoff admission of 10% of inactive atoms recovers 0.73 of the gap (random 0.11, position null negative); 0.71 of upstream decoder columns represented at a median of 5 atoms, 0.24 of encoder rows, 0.29 / 0.76 unreachable.
